```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 02_frequency_learning_checks
title: >
  Learning Checks
questions:
  - id: graph_types
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Which variable is most naturally shown with a bar graph rather than a
      histogram?
    options:
      - text: Marital-status categories
        correct: true
      - text: Test-score intervals
      - text: 50-millisecond reaction-time bins
      - text: Viewing time rounded to whole minutes
    explanation: >
      Marital status consists of separate categories, so a bar graph makes
      sense. The other options describe quantitative values arranged along a
      scale, which can be shown in adjacent histogram bins. Rounding continuous
      time to whole minutes does not turn it into a categorical variable.

  - id: grouped_reaction_time_n
    type: numeric
    prompt: |
      This grouped frequency table shows participants' reaction times.

      | Reaction time (milliseconds) | $f$ |
      |:-----------------------------|----:|
      | 200--249 | 3 |
      | 250--299 | 7 |
      | 300--349 | 9 |
      | 350--399 | 6 |

      How many participants were in the study?
    hint: >
      Each participant belongs to exactly one bin. Add the frequencies in the
      $f$ column.
    answer: 25
    tolerance: 0
    explanation: >
      The bins cover the observed scores without gaps or overlaps, so each
      participant is counted exactly once. Adding the frequencies gives
      $3 + 7 + 9 + 6 = 25$.

  - id: percentage_three_or_more_siblings
    type: numeric
    prompt: |
      This frequency table shows how many siblings a group of people reported.

      | Number of siblings | $f$ |
      |:-------------------|----:|
      | 0 | 2 |
      | 1 | 6 |
      | 2 | 7 |
      | 3 | 4 |
      | 4 | 1 |

      What percentage of people reported 3 or more siblings?
    hints:
      - >
        Add the frequencies for 3 and 4 siblings, then divide by the total
        frequency.
      - >
        There are $4 + 1 = 5$ people with 3 or more siblings out of 20 people
        altogether. Convert $5/20$ to a percentage.
    answer: 25
    tolerance: 0.1
    explanation: >
      The frequencies for 3 and 4 siblings add to 5. The total frequency is 20,
      so $5/20 \times 100 = 25\%$.

  - id: compare_class_distributions
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      A psychologist measures loneliness among first-year students who live on
      campus and first-year students who commute. We want to overlay the two
      distributions of loneliness scores so we can compare their shapes. Which
      graph is especially useful for this purpose?
    hint: >
      Think about whether several sets of bars or several lines can share the
      same axes without hiding one another.
    options:
      - text: >
          Bar graph
      - text: >
          Histogram
      - text: >
          Frequency polygon
        correct: true
      - text: >
          Pie chart
    explanation: >
      A frequency polygon is built from the same frequencies as a histogram,
      but several lines can be overlaid without obscuring one another as much as
      several sets of bars. A histogram could still describe either group on
      its own; the frequency polygon is a useful choice for this comparison,
      not a rule the data force us to follow.

  - id: grouped_table_information_loss
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      A grouped table places reaction times into 50-millisecond bins: 200--249,
      250--299, 300--349, and so on. Which information can we no longer recover
      from the grouped table alone?
    hint: >
      Ask what happens to the exact values once several of them are counted in
      the same row.
    options:
      - text: Total number of participants
      - text: Frequency in the 300--349 millisecond bin
      - text: Frequency at exactly 317 milliseconds
        correct: true
      - text: Most frequent bin
    explanation: >
      The table preserves the frequency in each bin, so we can still recover the
      total, compare bins, and identify the most frequent one. But it no longer
      shows how those observations were divided among the exact values within a
      bin.

  - id: smooth_curve_exact_frequencies
    type: true-false
    prompt: >
      A smooth curve based on a sample shows the exact observed frequency at
      every point along the scale.
    hint: >
      The curve fills in values between and around the observed scores. Were
      all of those values actually recorded?
    answer: false
    explanation: >
      False. A smooth curve models the shape between and around the observed
      scores; it is not a literal inventory of the sample. That can be useful
      when we use a sample to imagine a population, but the smoothness is part
      of the model rather than something we observed directly.
```
